parts.text:
Deciding which species deserve protection

An estimated 1 million species are currently threatened with extinction worldwide, and early

suggest the world is falling short on most of the agreement’s global biodiversity targets.

Because resources are limited, conservationists must weigh trade-offs in deciding which species to protect and how. Should they fund expensive

efforts for a species close to extinction, or interventions likely to help multiple species at once? Or maybe they should protect organisms that are unique to a specific geographic region or a species that sustains local livelihoods.

Some species are valued for what they do for

, such as pollinating crops or purifying water, known as ecosystem services. Honeybees, for example, pollinate over $15 billion worth of crops in the U.S. alone each year. Others hold cultural and spiritual significance, as the

does for the Yurok Tribe in California. Many conservationists argue that living species possess an inherent right to exist independent of their usefulness to human beings.

Getting support for measures to save charismatic species can be easier than for others, however. Think of Greenpeace’s “save the

” campaign or the World Wildlife Fund’s panda logo. A panda’s adorable face can help pay for its protection and potentially the protection of its surrounding habitat, helping other species living there.

A 2025 study examined more than 14,000 species-focused

projects from 1992 to 2016. Five mammal groups – primates, carnivores, whales, elephants and rhinos – received 86% of available funding, despite accounting for only one-third of threatened mammal projects. Plants and

, which are crucial for pollination, nutrient cycling and sustaining food webs, received only 6.6% of the financial backing.

Conservation groups and economists at the Paulson Institute estimate that the world needs to spend an additional $1.3

annually on biodiversity conservation and restoration to stop and reverse biodiversity loss.

Who bears the costs?

At the 2026 biodiversity conference, delegates will also take up another question that can make or break species

: When conservation affects local people, who pays and who gets a say?

While conservationists celebrated efforts to return wolves to Europe over the past two decades, some farmers lost livestock to these predators and faced higher costs to protect their
. Current European Union funding programs help support livestock protection, but farmers’ ability to shape wolf recovery is part of the story too.
